name: Facial feedback
statement: The arrangement of your own face feeds back into how you feel, so holding a smile makes things seem funnier even when you did not smile because of them.
meaning: The hypothesis reverses the usual direction. Instead of amusement producing a smile, the smile is held to produce some of the amusement. What made the idea testable was a way to arrange someone's face without telling them why: give them a pen to hold in their mouth. Held in the teeth it recruits the muscles of a smile, held in the lips it prevents one, and the participant thinks the study is about writing with your mouth. Any difference in how funny they find a cartoon afterwards cannot be explained by their knowing what expression they were making.

origin.who: Fritz Strack, Leonard L. Martin and Sabine Stepper
origin.where: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
origin.note: Their paper is titled "Inhibiting and facilitating conditions of the human smile: A nonobtrusive test of the facial feedback hypothesis". The pen manipulation is the reason it became one of the most reproduced demonstrations in undergraduate teaching.

evidence: Participants rate cartoons for funniness while holding a pen either in their teeth or in their lips. The original reported that the teeth group rated the cartoons 0.82 units higher on a ten-point scale. That single number carried a great deal: it is the demonstration cited when the facial feedback hypothesis is introduced, and until 2016 the study had never been directly replicated.

replication.headline: Seventeen laboratories ran the pen protocol on 1,894 people and the gap between smiling and pouting all but vanished.
replication.detail: The Registered Replication Report followed one vetted protocol at every site. Where the original found a 0.82-unit gap on its ten-point scale, the meta-analysis across all 17 labs found 0.03 units, with a 95% confidence interval from -0.11 to 0.16. The interval contains zero and excludes anything close to the original figure. It is worth being precise about what was tested: this is Study 1 of Strack and colleagues, run as they ran it, not the facial feedback hypothesis in general. Later work has argued that the effect may depend on conditions the protocol removed, including whether anyone is watching, and that argument is live rather than settled.

study.cite: Wagenmakers, E.-J., Beek, T., Dijkhoff, L., et al. (2016). Registered Replication Report: Strack, Martin, & Stepper (1988). Perspectives on Psychological Science, 11(6), 917-928.

limits: No confidence interval is printed for the original, because the 1988 paper's abstract is not available from Crossref or any open repository checked and the replication report quotes only its point estimate. The two numbers are also on the study's own rating scale rather than standardised, which is how both papers report them: converting to a standardised effect size would produce a figure neither source contains. And the comparison is between one original study and one protocol, however many laboratories ran it.
misreadings: The result is often stated as proof that facial expressions have no effect on emotion. It is narrower than that. What failed is one specific demonstration at the size it originally reported, and a hypothesis is not one experiment. A broader meta-analysis of the facial feedback literature has since concluded that effects on emotional experience exist but are small and variable, which is a different finding from either the 1988 paper or the 2016 report. The pen study is also still taught as an established result, which is the more common error: it is now the best-documented non-replication in the field.

sources.text: Strack, F., Martin, L. L., & Stepper, S. (1988). Inhibiting and facilitating conditions of the human smile: A nonobtrusive test of the facial feedback hypothesis. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 54(5), 768-777.
Wagenmakers, E.-J., Beek, T., Dijkhoff, L., et al. (2016). Registered Replication Report: Strack, Martin, & Stepper (1988). Perspectives on Psychological Science, 11(6), 917-928.
